claims.claim: NK1R-expressing neurons lying under the lateral edge of the facial nucleus and extending laterally out to the spinal trigeminal tract have respiratory-rhythmic burst activity from third trimester in utero to adulthood.
claims.source: From third trimester in utero to adulthood, NK1R-expressing neurons lying under the lateral edge of the facial nucleus and extending laterally out to the spinal trigeminal tract have respiratory-rhythmic burst activity (Onimaru et al., 2008; Thoby-Brisson et al., 2009; Pagliardini et al., 2011; Huckstepp et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is stated with citations to multiple studies.

claims.claim: In E14.5 mice, neurons under the lateral edge of the facial nucleus are designated as comprising the embryonic parafacial nucleus (e-pF).
claims.source: In E14.5 mice, these neurons are designated as comprising the embryonic parafacial nucleus (e-pF) (Thoby-Brisson et al., 2009); in postnatal rats, these neurons are designated as comprising the parafacial respiratory group (pFRG) (Onimaru and Homma, 2003), and; in the adult rat, these neurons are designated as comprising the pFL (Pagliardini et al., 2011; Huckstepp et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is stated with citation to Thoby-Brisson et al., 2009.

claims.claim: In postnatal rats, neurons under the lateral edge of the facial nucleus are designated as comprising the parafacial respiratory group (pFRG).
claims.source: In E14.5 mice, these neurons are designated as comprising the embryonic parafacial nucleus (e-pF) (Thoby-Brisson et al., 2009); in postnatal rats, these neurons are designated as comprising the parafacial respiratory group (pFRG) (Onimaru and Homma, 2003), and; in the adult rat, these neurons are designated as comprising the pFL (Pagliardini et al., 2011; Huckstepp et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is stated with citation to Onimaru and Homma, 2003.

claims.claim: In the adult rat, neurons under the lateral edge of the facial nucleus are designated as comprising the pFL.
claims.source: In E14.5 mice, these neurons are designated as comprising the embryonic parafacial nucleus (e-pF) (Thoby-Brisson et al., 2009); in postnatal rats, these neurons are designated as comprising the parafacial respiratory group (pFRG) (Onimaru and Homma, 2003), and; in the adult rat, these neurons are designated as comprising the pFL (Pagliardini et al., 2011; Huckstepp et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is stated with citations to Pagliardini et al., 2011 and Huckstepp et al., 2015.

claims.claim: The most parsimonious interpretation is that one population of neurons exists in sequence within the homologous anatomical location at distinctly different developmental time points (e-pF, pFRG, pFL).
claims.source: While 3 distinctly different groups of NK1R neurons expressing respiratory-rhythmic bursting could exist in sequence within this homologous anatomical location at distinctly different developmental time points, the most parsimonious interpretation is of one population of neurons studied at different developmental time points; we postulate that this is the case.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a postulate based on parsimony.

claims.claim: NK1R-expressing neurons in the ventral respiratory column (including the parafacial region) are almost exclusively glutamatergic.
claims.source: NK1R-expressing neurons in the ventral respiratory column (including the parafacial region) are almost exclusively glutamatergic (Guyenet et al., 2002).
claims.evidence: This is stated with citation to Guyenet et al., 2002.

claims.claim: In embryonic and postnatal rodents, the pFL is comprised of glutamatergic NK1R-expressing neurons.
claims.source: In embryonic and postnatal rodents, the pFL is comprised of glutamatergic NK1R-expressing neurons (Onimaru et al., 2008; Thoby-Brisson et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This is stated with citations to Onimaru et al., 2008 and Thoby-Brisson et al., 2009.

claims.claim: In the adult rodent, the presumptive pFL expiratory oscillator is comprised (mostly) of NK1R-expressing neurons.
claims.source: In the adult rodent, the presumptive pFL expiratory oscillator is comprised (mostly) of NK1R-expressing neurons (Figure 1D, see also Huckstepp et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is stated with reference to Figure 1D and citation to Huckstepp et al., 2015.

claims.claim: The pFL and pFV do not appear to contain any inhibitory neurons.
claims.source: Since the pFL and pFV do not appear to contain any inhibitory neurons (Ellenberger, 1999; Stornetta and Guyenet, 1999; Tanaka et al., 2003; Fortuna et al., 2008; Abbott et al., 2009), we conclude that any resultant inhibitory action associated with their activity occurs through an intermediate relay of inhibitory neurons, perhaps located in the preBötC (Morgado-Valle et al., 2010) or BötC (Schreihofer et al., 1999).
claims.evidence: This is stated with citations to multiple studies.

claims.claim: Any resultant inhibitory action associated with pFL and pFV activity occurs through an intermediate relay of inhibitory neurons, perhaps located in the preBötC or BötC.
claims.source: Since the pFL and pFV do not appear to contain any inhibitory neurons (Ellenberger, 1999; Stornetta and Guyenet, 1999; Tanaka et al., 2003; Fortuna et al., 2008; Abbott et al., 2009), we conclude that any resultant inhibitory action associated with their activity occurs through an intermediate relay of inhibitory neurons, perhaps located in the preBötC (Morgado-Valle et al., 2010) or BötC (Schreihofer et al., 1999).
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the absence of inhibitory neurons in pFL and pFV, with citations to studies on inhibitory neurons in preBötC and BötC.

claims.claim: In E14.5 mice, the pFL is rhythmic before the preBötC appears to form.
claims.source: In E14.5 mice, the pFL is rhythmic before the preBötC appears to form (Figure 9Ai; see also Thoby-Brisson et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This is stated with reference to Figure 9Ai and citation to Thoby-Brisson et al., 2009.

claims.claim: At E15.5, the preBötC forms and becomes rhythmically coupled to the pFL.
claims.source: At E15.5, the preBötC forms (Thoby-Brisson et al., 2005) and it becomes rhythmically coupled to the pFL (Thoby-Brisson et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This is stated with citations to Thoby-Brisson et al., 2005 and 2009.

claims.claim: At E15.5, the preBötC and pFL can oscillate independently following a transverse section caudal to facial nucleus.
claims.source: At this time: i) the preBötC and pFL can oscillate independently following a transverse section caudal to facial nucleus (Figure 9Aiii); ii) the pFL can oscillate in the absence of preBötC rhythm following bath application of the glutamatergic antagonist CNQX (Figure 9Aiv), and; iii) the preBötC can oscillate in the absence of the pFL following administration of the sodium channel blocker riluzole (Figure 9Av) (Thoby-Brisson et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This is stated with reference to Figure 9Aiii and citation to Thoby-Brisson et al., 2009.

claims.claim: At E15.5, the pFL can oscillate in the absence of preBötC rhythm following bath application of the glutamatergic antagonist CNQX.
claims.source: At this time: i) the preBötC and pFL can oscillate independently following a transverse section caudal to facial nucleus (Figure 9Aiii); ii) the pFL can oscillate in the absence of preBötC rhythm following bath application of the glutamatergic antagonist CNQX (Figure 9Aiv), and; iii) the preBötC can oscillate in the absence of the pFL following administration of the sodium channel blocker riluzole (Figure 9Av) (Thoby-Brisson et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This is stated with reference to Figure 9Aiv and citation to Thoby-Brisson et al., 2009.

claims.claim: At E15.5, the preBötC can oscillate in the absence of the pFL following administration of the sodium channel blocker riluzole.
claims.source: At this time: i) the preBötC and pFL can oscillate independently following a transverse section caudal to facial nucleus (Figure 9Aiii); ii) the pFL can oscillate in the absence of preBötC rhythm following bath application of the glutamatergic antagonist CNQX (Figure 9Aiv), and; iii) the preBötC can oscillate in the absence of the pFL following administration of the sodium channel blocker riluzole (Figure 9Av) (Thoby-Brisson et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This is stated with reference to Figure 9Av and citation to Thoby-Brisson et al., 2009.

claims.claim: Embryonically, the preBötC and pFL are independent, coupled oscillators, and rhythmic output of the network is a convolution of the faster rhythm of the pFL and the slower rhythm of the preBötC.
claims.source: Thus embryonically, the preBötC and pFL are independent, coupled oscillators, and rhythmic output of the network is a convolution of the faster rhythm of the pFL and the slower rhythm of the preBötC (Thoby-Brisson et al., 2009); the pFL (Thoby-Brisson et al., 2009) provides excitatory drive to the preBötC, while bursting in the preBötC, comprised of inhibitory (Rahman et al., 2015) and excitatory neuronal activity (Gray et al., 2010), inhibits and excites pFL neurons (Thoby-Brisson et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This is stated with citation to Thoby-Brisson et al., 2009.

claims.claim: Embryonically, the pFL provides excitatory drive to the preBötC.
claims.source: Thus embryonically, the preBötC and pFL are independent, coupled oscillators, and rhythmic output of the network is a convolution of the faster rhythm of the pFL and the slower rhythm of the preBötC (Thoby-Brisson et al., 2009); the pFL (Thoby-Brisson et al., 2009) provides excitatory drive to the preBötC, while bursting in the preBötC, comprised of inhibitory (Rahman et al., 2015) and excitatory neuronal activity (Gray et al., 2010), inhibits and excites pFL neurons (Thoby-Brisson et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This is stated with citation to Thoby-Brisson et al., 2009.

claims.claim: Embryonically, bursting in the preBötC, comprised of inhibitory and excitatory neuronal activity, inhibits and excites pFL neurons.
claims.source: Thus embryonically, the preBötC and pFL are independent, coupled oscillators, and rhythmic output of the network is a convolution of the faster rhythm of the pFL and the slower rhythm of the preBötC (Thoby-Brisson et al., 2009); the pFL (Thoby-Brisson et al., 2009) provides excitatory drive to the preBötC, while bursting in the preBötC, comprised of inhibitory (Rahman et al., 2015) and excitatory neuronal activity (Gray et al., 2010), inhibits and excites pFL neurons (Thoby-Brisson et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This is stated with citations to Rahman et al., 2015, Gray et al., 2010, and Thoby-Brisson et al., 2009.

claims.claim: In postnatal rats, the glutamatergic pFL provides excitatory drive to the preBötC.
claims.source: In postnatal rats, respiratory rhythm appears similar to the embryo; the glutamatergic pFL provides excitatory drive to the preBötC (Onimaru and Homma, 2003; Onimaru et al., 2012), while bursting of the preBötC, comprised of inhibitory (Morgado-Valle et al., 2010) and excitatory neurons (Gray et al., 2010), inhibits and excites different subsets of pFL neurons (Takeda et al., 2001; Onimaru et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: This is stated with citations to Onimaru and Homma, 2003 and Onimaru et al., 2012.

claims.claim: In postnatal rats, bursting of the preBötC, comprised of inhibitory and excitatory neurons, inhibits and excites different subsets of pFL neurons.
claims.source: In postnatal rats, respiratory rhythm appears similar to the embryo; the glutamatergic pFL provides excitatory drive to the preBötC (Onimaru and Homma, 2003; Onimaru et al., 2012), while bursting of the preBötC, comprised of inhibitory (Morgado-Valle et al., 2010) and excitatory neurons (Gray et al., 2010), inhibits and excites different subsets of pFL neurons (Takeda et al., 2001; Onimaru et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: This is stated with citations to Morgado-Valle et al., 2010, Gray et al., 2010, Takeda et al., 2001, and Onimaru et al., 2007.

claims.claim: In postnatal rats, the preBötC can oscillate in transverse slices, i.e., in the absence of the pFL.
claims.source: At this time: i) the preBötC can oscillate in transverse slices, i.e., in the absence of the pFL (Figure 9Bi) (Smith et al., 1991) and; ii) the pFL can oscillate following suppression of preBötC rhythm by bath application of opioid agonists (Figure 9Bii) (Takeda et al., 2001; Janczewski et al., 2002).
claims.evidence: This is stated with reference to Figure 9Bi and citation to Smith et al., 1991.

claims.claim: In postnatal rats, the pFL can oscillate following suppression of preBötC rhythm by bath application of opioid agonists.
claims.source: At this time: i) the preBötC can oscillate in transverse slices, i.e., in the absence of the pFL (Figure 9Bi) (Smith et al., 1991) and; ii) the pFL can oscillate following suppression of preBötC rhythm by bath application of opioid agonists (Figure 9Bii) (Takeda et al., 2001; Janczewski et al., 2002).
claims.evidence: This is stated with reference to Figure 9Bii and citations to Takeda et al., 2001 and Janczewski et al., 2002.

claims.claim: Postnatally, the preBötC and pFL are independent, coupled oscillators.
claims.source: Thus postnatally, the preBötC and pFL are also independent, coupled oscillators.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the evidence presented about postnatal respiratory control.

claims.claim: Immediately following birth, respiratory rhythm appears driven by the pFL.
claims.source: Immediately following birth, respiratory rhythm appears driven by the pFL (Figure 9Biii) (Onimaru and Homma, 2003; Oku et al., 2007), perhaps to protect against the opioid surge in the fetal brain during birth (Janczewski et al., 2002) that would act to suppress preBötC activity (Takeda et al., 2001).
claims.evidence: This is stated with reference to Figure 9Biii and citations to Onimaru and Homma, 2003 and Oku et al., 2007.

claims.claim: The pFL may drive respiratory rhythm immediately following birth to protect against the opioid surge in the fetal brain during birth that would act to suppress preBötC activity.
claims.source: Immediately following birth, respiratory rhythm appears driven by the pFL (Figure 9Biii) (Onimaru and Homma, 2003; Oku et al., 2007), perhaps to protect against the opioid surge in the fetal brain during birth (Janczewski et al., 2002) that would act to suppress preBötC activity (Takeda et al., 2001).
claims.evidence: This is stated as a speculation with citations to Janczewski et al., 2002 and Takeda et al., 2001.

claims.claim: Shortly after birth (~P2-P4), the breathing central pattern generator (CPG) matures, and becomes driven by the preBötC.
claims.source: Shortly after birth (~P2-P4), the breathing central pattern generator (CPG) matures, and becomes driven by the preBötC (Oku et al., 2007; Mckay et al., 2009; Kennedy, 2015) (Figure 9Biv), and remains so throughout life.
claims.evidence: This is stated with reference to Figure 9Biv and citations to Oku et al., 2007, Mckay et al., 2009, and Kennedy, 2015.

claims.claim: The breathing CPG remains driven by the preBötC throughout life after ~P2-P4.
claims.source: Shortly after birth (~P2-P4), the breathing central pattern generator (CPG) matures, and becomes driven by the preBötC (Oku et al., 2007; Mckay et al., 2009; Kennedy, 2015) (Figure 9Biv), and remains so throughout life.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on the cited literature.

claims.claim: In juvenile rats, the preBötC and pFL are reciprocally coupled but are still differentially affected by fentanyl, which shifts breathing to an expiratory-dominant pattern.
claims.source: In juvenile rats, the preBötC and pFL are reciprocally coupled (9Ci) but are still differentially affected by fentanyl, which shifts breathing to an expiratory-dominant pattern (9Cii) (Janczewski and Feldman, 2006).
claims.evidence: This is stated with reference to Figure 9Ci-ii and citation to Janczewski and Feldman, 2006.

claims.claim: In juvenile rats, the preBötC and pFL can be independently suppressed by the Breuer-Hering deflation reflex (BHDR) or inflation reflex (BHIR).
claims.source: Also, the preBötC and pFL can be independently suppressed by the Breuer-Hering deflation reflex (BHDR; 9Cii) or inflation reflex (BHIR; 9Ciii) (Janczewski and Feldman, 2006).
claims.evidence: This is stated with reference to Figure 9Cii-iii and citation to Janczewski and Feldman, 2006.

claims.claim: In adult rats, the preBötC is the dominant oscillator, active at rest to drive inspiratory movements.
claims.source: The preBötC is the dominant oscillator, active at rest to drive inspiratory movements (Figure 9Di, see also Pagliardini et al., 2011 and Huckstepp et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is stated with reference to Figure 9Di and citations to Pagliardini et al., 2011 and Huckstepp et al., 2015.

claims.claim: In adult rats, the pFL is the subsidiary conditional oscillator, quiescent at rest.
claims.source: The pFL is the subsidiary conditional oscillator, quiescent at rest (Figure 9Di); in the presence of concurrent, or reduced, preBötC activity (Figure 2), and appropriate inputs, such as an increase in expiratory drive through activation of exogenous receptors (Figure 6, see also Pagliardini et al., 2011) or altered blood gases (Huckstepp et al., 2015), the pFL drives active expiration (Figure 9Dii).
claims.evidence: This is stated with reference to Figure 9Di.

claims.claim: In adult rats, in the presence of concurrent, or reduced, preBötC activity and appropriate inputs, such as an increase in expiratory drive through activation of exogenous receptors or altered blood gases, the pFL drives active expiration.
claims.source: The pFL is the subsidiary conditional oscillator, quiescent at rest (Figure 9Di); in the presence of concurrent, or reduced, preBötC activity (Figure 2), and appropriate inputs, such as an increase in expiratory drive through activation of exogenous receptors (Figure 6, see also Pagliardini et al., 2011) or altered blood gases (Huckstepp et al., 2015), the pFL drives active expiration (Figure 9Dii).
claims.evidence: This is stated with references to Figures 2, 6, and 9Dii, and citations to Pagliardini et al., 2011 and Huckstepp et al., 2015.

claims.claim: In adult rats, in the absence of preBötC activity, chemosensory drive increases network excitability and drives active expiration, though abdominal activity is tonic due to a lack of phasic inhibition from the preBötC.
claims.source: In the absence of preBötC activity, chemosensory drive increases network excitability and drives active expiration, though abdominal activity is tonic due to a lack of phasic inhibition from the preBötC (Figure 9Diii).
claims.evidence: This is stated with reference to Figure 9Diii and is based on the experimental data.

claims.claim: In adult rats, the pFL appears incapable of independently driving respiratory movements when preBötC activity is silenced by exogenous receptors.
claims.source: However, the pFL appears incapable of independently driving respiratory movements in the adult rat when preBötC activity is silenced by exogenous receptors (Figures 2, 7, 9Div) or when preBötC activity is low and blood gases are normal (Figures 8, 9Dv).
claims.evidence: This is stated with references to Figures 2, 7, 8, and 9Div-v.

claims.claim: In adult rats, the pFL appears incapable of independently driving respiratory movements when preBötC activity is low and blood gases are normal.
claims.source: However, the pFL appears incapable of independently driving respiratory movements in the adult rat when preBötC activity is silenced by exogenous receptors (Figures 2, 7, 9Div) or when preBötC activity is low and blood gases are normal (Figures 8, 9Dv).
claims.evidence: This is stated with references to Figures 8 and 9Dv.

claims.claim: As preBötC neurons project to the pFV but do not appear to project to the pFL, excitatory drive from the preBötC to the pFL is most likely through an intermediate excitatory relay, such as the pFV.
claims.source: As preBötC neurons project to the pFV but do not appear to project to the pFL (Tan et al., 2010), excitatory drive from the preBötC to the pFL is most likely through an intermediate excitatory relay, such as the pFV (Figure 9Dii).
claims.evidence: This is stated with reference to Figure 9Dii and citation to Tan et al., 2010.

claims.claim: Lowered drive in the preBötC from activation of the allatostatin receptor creates burstlets in the preBötC.
claims.source: Here, lowered drive in the preBötC from activation of the allatostatin receptor creates burstlets in the preBötC; under normal conditions these burstlet signals are not strong enough to drive motor activity.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data.

claims.claim: Under normal conditions, burstlet signals in the preBötC are not strong enough to drive motor activity.
claims.source: Here, lowered drive in the preBötC from activation of the allatostatin receptor creates burstlets in the preBötC; under normal conditions these burstlet signals are not strong enough to drive motor activity.
claims.evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of normal physiology.

claims.claim: Increased excitability in the premotor and motor network caused by increased chemosensory drive causes normally subthreshold burstlet events to become suprathreshold, and thus these burstlets are transmitted to the motor output.
claims.source: However, increased excitability in the premotor and motor network caused by increased chemosensory drive (from decreased ventilation) causes these normally subthreshold events to become suprathreshold, and thus these burstlets are transmitted to the motor output.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data.

claims.claim: During quantal slowing of breathing, inspiratory activity on the DiaEMG and GGEMG was interspersed with AbdEMG activity.

results.result: Viral transfection successfully targeted the preBötC and pFL with high specificity. From preBötC injection sites, 82±6% of neurons expressed GFP (n=3), and from pFL injection sites, 81±3% expressed mCitrine (n=3). Transfection sites ranged from ~350–600 µm in diameter, with no labeling found outside injection sites, including the Bötzinger complex.
results.evaluation: Claims C26-C32 provide direct histological measurements demonstrating successful and specific viral transfection. The high transfection efficiency (>80%), lack of off-target labeling, and independence of responses from injection site size (C29-C30) collectively support the specificity and validity of the targeting approach.

results.result: Hyperpolarizing preBötC neurons via Alst injection decreased breathing frequency (42 to 22 breaths/min, p=0.008), increased TI and TE, decreased VT and ∫DiaEMG, and induced active expiration during mild hypercapnia. The frequency decrease was quantal rather than continuous, with burstlets appearing during longer respiratory periods. Ultimately, inspiratory activity ceased, leading to apnea.
results.evaluation: Claims C33-C45 present comprehensive experimental data with appropriate statistical tests (p-values reported, n=8) showing the effects of preBötC silencing. The quantal slowing pattern (C41-C42) is supported by kernel density analysis, and the appearance of burstlets (C43-C44) is documented in Figures 2-3. The progression from decreased breathing to active expiration to apnea is well-documented.

results.result: Control experiments in non-transfected rats (n=8) showed that Alst injection into the preBötC had no effect on any respiratory parameters (all p>0.1), confirming that the effects observed in transfected rats resulted specifically from AlstR activation.
results.evaluation: Claims C46-C53 provide essential negative controls demonstrating specificity of the AlstR system. The lack of effects in non-transfected animals (n=8, appropriate statistical tests) validates that observed effects in transfected animals are due to receptor activation rather than non-specific drug effects.

results.result: Control experiments in non-transfected rats (n=8) showed that 90 µM CNO had no effect on any respiratory parameters (all p>0.1), confirming the specificity of the HM3DR system.
results.evaluation: Claims C54-C61 provide essential negative controls for the CNO/HM3DR system. The lack of effects in non-transfected animals (n=8, appropriate statistical tests) validates that observed effects in transfected animals are due to receptor activation rather than non-specific drug effects.

results.result: Depolarizing pFL neurons via CNO (90 µM) in HM3DR-transfected rats (n=8) increased breathing frequency (37 to 42 breaths/min, p=0.04), decreased TE, increased VT, ∫DiaEMG, and ∫GGEMG, and induced expiratory-related ∫AbdEMG (p=0.02), confirming that pFL activation produces active expiration.
results.evaluation: Claims C62-C70 present comprehensive experimental data with appropriate statistical tests (n=8) showing that pFL activation induces active expiration. The results are consistent with prior optogenetic studies (C69), providing convergent evidence for the role of pFL in active expiration.

results.result: When pFL neurons were activated by CNO and preBötC neurons were subsequently silenced by Alst, respiratory activity decreased and ultimately resulted in apnea. After inspiratory activity ceased, ∫AbdEMG continued tonically for 15±12 s before disappearing, with rats becoming severely hypercapnic (ETCO2 64.6±14.5 mm Hg).
results.evaluation: Claims C71-C75 present experimental data (n=8, p=0.008) showing that pFL activation alone cannot sustain active expiration when preBötC is silenced. The tonic AbdEMG duration and hypercapnia levels are well-documented, with appropriate statistical comparisons to control conditions (p=0.7, p=0.8).

results.result: During recovery from apnea (with CNO-activated pFL and Alst-silenced preBötC), inspiratory activity always returned before expiratory activity. Active expiration did not return until VT reached 3.2±1.7 mL, ∫DiaEMG reached 13.1±8.2 a.u., and ∫GGEMG reached 5.2±4.2 a.u. (n=8). At no time did active expiration occur in the absence of inspiratory activity and chemosensory drive.
results.evaluation: Claims C76-C79 present critical experimental observations (n=8) demonstrating that pFL cannot independently drive active expiration without preBötC activity or chemosensory drive. The threshold values for active expiration return are quantified, and the consistent temporal sequence (inspiration before expiration) is well-documented in Figure 8.

results.result: The authors conclude that in adult rats, active expiration is driven by the pFL but requires additional network excitation from either ongoing rhythmic preBötC activity sufficient to drive inspiratory motor output or increased chemosensory drive. The preBötC is the dominant oscillator while the pFL is a subsidiary conditional oscillator, establishing an asymmetrical rather than symmetrical half-center organization.
results.evaluation: Claims C8, C25, C135, C153-C159 represent the main conclusions synthesized from the experimental data. The conclusion that pFL requires additional excitation is directly supported by the inability to induce active expiration when preBötC is silenced and blood gases are normal (C76-C79, C151-C152). The hierarchical organization is supported by the differential capabilities of the two oscillators demonstrated throughout the experiments.

results.result: Depressing preBötC activity resulted in quantal slowing of breathing, with burstlets appearing on inspiratory muscle EMGs and airflow during longer respiratory periods. These burstlets represent low-level rhythmogenic activity in the preBötC that, under conditions of increased chemosensory drive, become suprathreshold and are transmitted to motor output.
results.evaluation: Claims C21-C23, C41-C44, C122-C127 describe the quantal slowing phenomenon and burstlet transmission. The quantal nature is supported by kernel density analysis (C42, Figure 3C), and the appearance of burstlets is documented in Figures 2-3 and 7. The interpretation is consistent with prior work (Kam et al., 2013) and supported by the observation that burstlets can inhibit AbdEMG even when expiratory activity is high (C126).

results.result: Following hyperpolarization of preBötC neurons, active expiration appeared, potentially due to increased hypoxic/hypercapnic drive to the pFL or disinhibition of the pFL from loss of inhibitory preBötC drive. Subsequently, when inspiratory motor outflow disappeared and hypercapnia/hypoxia increased, active expiration ceased, possibly due to severe hypoxia inhibiting expiratory motor output.
results.evaluation: Claims C128-C133 present observations (C128 is supported by data) but offer speculative mechanistic explanations (C131-C133). While the appearance of active expiration is documented, the authors acknowledge uncertainty about whether it results from chemosensory drive or disinhibition (C130). The cessation of active expiration during severe hypoxia is observed but the mechanism remains speculative.

results.result: As rats transitioned from eupnea to apnea following preBötC suppression, ∫AbdEMG transitioned from phasic to tonic. The authors suggest this occurs because expiratory activity is phasic due to periodic inhibition during inspiration, becoming tonic once phasic inspiratory inhibition is lost due to silencing of inhibitory preBötC neurons, implying a significant role for inhibitory preBötC neurons in shaping expiratory output.
results.evaluation: Claims C136-C142 present observations (C136-C137, C142 are well-documented in Figures 2, 7, 9) and interpretations (C139-C141). The phasic-to-tonic transition is clearly demonstrated, and the interpretation is supported by comparison with prior work in cats (C138, Sears et al., 1982) and by citations to studies on inhibitory preBötC neurons (C140). The asymmetry between eupnea-to-apnea and apnea-to-eupnea transitions (C142) provides additional support.

results.result: Following apnea during mechanical ventilation (with CNO-activated pFL and Alst-silenced preBötC), breathing recovery occurred in three phases: (1) no activity even off ventilator, (2) spontaneous breathing only when off ventilator (likely due to chemosensory drive overcoming waning Alst effect), and (3) spontaneous breathing during ventilation once Alst wore off. In all phases, inspiratory activity returned before expiratory activity, and active expiration never occurred without inspiration. Since blood gases were normal, the loss of expiratory activity was not due to excessive hypoxia/hypercapnia.
results.evaluation: Claims C143-C152 describe detailed observations from the recovery protocol (n=8, documented in Figure 8). The three-phase recovery pattern is well-documented, and the consistent temporal sequence (inspiration before expiration) is clearly demonstrated. The inference that normal blood gases rule out hypoxia/hypercapnia as the cause (C152) is reasonable given the measurements shown in Figure 8.

results.result: The authors address the potential confound of retrograde transfection by AAV2/5, asserting that results are unlikely to be confounded because: (1) no labeling was found outside injection sites, (2) CNO was applied to the ventral surface with limited penetration, and (3) effects match those from optogenetic studies using non-retrogradely transported lentivirus.
results.evaluation: Claims C80-C85 address an important methodological concern. The evidence against retrograde transfection confounds is strong: histological analysis shows no off-target labeling (C82, Figure 1E-F), the drug application method limits spread (C83), and convergent results with optogenetics using lentivirus (C85) provide independent validation. However, the claim about limited CNO penetration (C83) is an inference rather than direct measurement.

results.result: The manuscript is based on the hypothesis that breathing in mammals results from interaction of two oscillators: the preBötC driving inspiration and the pFL driving active expiration. In mammals at rest, the preBötC drives the underlying rhythm, while the pFL turns on during increased metabolic demand. In adult rats, the preBötC can generate inspiratory rhythm while the pFL is quiescent.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C2, C9-C10, C16-C18 establish the conceptual framework based on prior literature. These claims are well-supported by extensive citations and represent established knowledge in the field. The experimental work in this manuscript tests and refines this framework.

results.result: NK1R-expressing neurons in the parafacial region show respiratory-rhythmic activity from third trimester in utero to adulthood. These neurons have been designated as e-pF (embryonic), pFRG (postnatal), and pFL (adult) at different developmental stages. The authors postulate these represent one population studied at different time points. These neurons are almost exclusively glutamatergic.
results.evaluation: Claims C86-C93 synthesize prior literature about the developmental identity of parafacial respiratory neurons. The claims are well-supported by multiple citations (C86-C89, C91-C92), and the parsimonious interpretation of a single population (C90) is reasonable though explicitly stated as a postulate. The glutamatergic nature is supported by citation (C91) and the authors' own data (C93, Figure 1D).

results.result: In embryonic mice, the pFL is rhythmic before the preBötC forms (E14.5). At E15.5, the preBötC forms and couples to the pFL. The two oscillators can function independently (demonstrated by transverse section, CNQX, or riluzole), and their rhythmic output is a convolution of the faster pFL and slower preBötC rhythms. The pFL provides excitatory drive to the preBötC, while preBötC bursting (inhibitory and excitatory) both inhibits and excites pFL neurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C96-C103 summarize prior work on embryonic respiratory control, primarily from Thoby-Brisson et al., 2009. These claims are well-supported by citations and Figure 9A provides a clear schematic. The claims accurately represent the cited literature.

results.result: In postnatal rats, the glutamatergic pFL provides excitatory drive to the preBötC, while preBötC bursting inhibits and excites different pFL neuron subsets. Both oscillators can function independently (preBötC in transverse slices, pFL after opioid suppression of preBötC). Immediately after birth, the pFL appears to drive respiratory rhythm, possibly to protect against opioid surge during birth. Shortly after birth (~P2-P4), the breathing CPG becomes driven by the preBötC and remains so throughout life.
results.evaluation: Claims C104-C112 summarize prior work on postnatal respiratory control with appropriate citations. The developmental transition from pFL-driven to preBötC-driven breathing is well-documented in the cited literature. The speculation about opioid protection (C110) is appropriately qualified. Figure 9B provides clear schematic support.

results.result: In juvenile rats, the preBötC and pFL are reciprocally coupled but differentially affected by fentanyl (shifts to expiratory-dominant pattern) and can be independently suppressed by Breuer-Hering reflexes (BHDR or BHIR).
results.evaluation: Claims C113-C114 summarize prior work from Janczewski and Feldman, 2006, with appropriate citation and schematic support in Figure 9C. These claims accurately represent the cited literature.

results.result: In adult rats, the preBötC is the dominant oscillator active at rest, while the pFL is a subsidiary conditional oscillator that is quiescent at rest. The pFL drives active expiration when preBötC activity is concurrent or reduced and appropriate inputs are present (exogenous receptor activation or altered blood gases). In the absence of preBötC activity, chemosensory drive can drive active expiration, though abdominal activity becomes tonic. The pFL cannot independently drive respiratory movements when preBötC is silenced or when preBötC activity is low with normal blood gases. Excitatory drive from preBötC to pFL likely occurs through an intermediate relay such as the pFV.
results.evaluation: Claims C115-C121 synthesize the current study's findings with prior work. The dominant/subsidiary oscillator relationship is directly supported by the experimental data (particularly C76-C79, C119-C120). The role of chemosensory drive (C118) is supported by the tonic AbdEMG during severe hypercapnia. The indirect connectivity through pFV (C121) is a reasonable inference based on anatomical data (Tan et al., 2010) and is appropriately qualified as "most likely."

results.result: The authors speculate that the asymmetrical organization of respiratory oscillators may be relevant to other neural networks with hierarchically organized coupled oscillators, such as those underlying flexion and extension in locomotion. The developmental and state-dependent changes in preBötC-pFL interactions represent additional complexity in understanding respiratory control.
results.evaluation: Claims C160-C161 present broader implications and perspectives. C160 is appropriately qualified as speculative ("may be relevant") with citations to locomotion literature.
